Breaking: Local Researchers Discover New Catalyst

By Imani Reyes · March 5, 2026

A team of chemists at the Bryden Institute have demonstrated a new copper-iron alloy catalyst that converts carbon dioxide into ethanol with 81 percent efficiency at room temperature, a result that could substantially reduce the energy cost of carbon recycling.

The catalyst, described this week in Nature Catalysis, sidesteps the precious-metal requirements of earlier approaches. "We were not expecting it to work at all," said lead author Dr. Petra Lunde, "and certainly not without heating."

How it works

The alloy presents a tiled nano-surface that traps CO₂ molecules in a configuration favorable to two-step reduction. When a low-voltage current is applied, the trapped molecules accept electrons and rearrange into ethanol with only trace methanol as byproduct.

The implications for industrial carbon capture are immediate, but scaling will require new manufacturing methods for the alloy itself.

What comes next

Lunde's team has partnered with two industrial firms to build a pilot reactor by the end of 2027. Independent replication is already underway in laboratories in Kyoto and Zurich.

Funding for the work came from the National Science Foundation and the Bryden Family Trust.
